# Background

## Introduction
\begin{itemize}
\item March Madness is the NCAA Division I Basketball Tournament, a single-elimination bracket of $68$ teams held each March and April across both the Men's and Women's divisions to crown the National Champions.
\vspace{0.1in}
\item Teams earn a spot either by winning their conference tournament (an automatic bid) or by being selected by the NCAA Selection Committee (an at-large bid).
\vspace{0.1in}
\item The regular season determines the seeding. Teams are seeded 1 through 16 within each of four regions, where lower seeds are considered the strongest and are rewarded with matchups against the highest seeds.
\vspace{0.1in}
\item With 63 games decided by single elimination, upsets are frequent, which is why the tournament has become famous for its unpredictability, hence the name ``March Madness.''
\end{itemize}

## Kaggle
\begin{itemize}
\item Kaggle is an online platform for data science and machine learning competitions, owned by Google.
\vspace{0.1in}
\item  Companies, researchers, and organizations post prediction problems with datasets, evaluation metrics, and prize pools.
\vspace{0.1in}
\item Participants submit models that are scored on a hidden test set, with a public leaderboard ranking submissions in real time.
\vspace{0.1in}
\item Kaggle has become a benchmark in the ML community for evaluating predictive modeling approaches against a global field of competitors.
\end{itemize}

## March Machine Learning Mania
\begin{itemize}
\item Annual Kaggle competition running since 2014, challenging participants to predict outcomes of every possible matchup in the NCAA tournament.
\vspace{0.2in}
\item Submissions are a probability $p \in [0,1]$ for each of the $4556$ possible matchups across Men's and Women's.
\vspace{0.2in} 
\item Scored using the Brier Score:
\begin{equation}
BS = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^N(f_t - o_t)^2
\end{equation}
\item Where $f_t$ is our prediction and $o_t$ is the outcome. 
\item $o_t$ is $1$ if the team wins, and $0$ is they lose. 
\end{itemize}

## Brier Score
\begin{itemize}
\item A naive 'coin flip' strategy (50\% probability for all games) yields a Brier Score of 0.25, serving as our baseline.
    \vspace{0.2in}
\end{itemize}
\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lllr}
\hline
\textbf{Predicted} & \textbf{Outcome} & \textbf{Scenario} & \textbf{Brier Score} \\
\hline
0.50 & Win or Loss & Baseline & 0.2500 \\
1.00 & Win         & Perfectly confident, correct   & 0.0000 \\
1.00 & Loss        & Perfectly confident, incorrect & 1.0000 \\
0.70 & Win         & Moderately confident, correct  & 0.0900 \\
0.70 & Loss        & Moderately confident, incorrect & 0.4900 \\
0.90 & Win         & Highly confident, correct      & 0.0100 \\
0.90 & Loss        & Highly confident, incorrect    & 0.8100 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\caption{Brier Score Examples}
\label{tab:brier}
\end{table}

## Prediction Difficulty
\begin{itemize}
\item Top predictive models plateau near $75\%$ accuracy \cite{Zimmermann}.
\vspace{0.2in}
\item Odds of a perfect bracket: $1$ in $9.2$ quintillion (random) to $1$ in $128$ billion (informed).
\vspace{0.2in}
\item No publicly verified bracket has survived past the Sweet Sixteen \cite{Bergen2018}.
\vspace{0.2in}
\item \$$3.1$ billion wagered in 2025, sportsbook lines are the benchmark to beat \cite{AGA2025}.
\end{itemize}

## Data Considerations
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{2020 Tournament Gap:} the COVID-canceled tournament produces no playoff observations; regular season $2020$ data is still usable.
\vspace{0.15in}
\item \textbf{Completeness:} no missing values across Kaggle, KenPom, or Torvik. Every team has a complete statistical profile.
\vspace{0.15in}
\item \textbf{Team Name Matching:} external sources use inconsistent spellings (ex: ``St.\ Mary's'' vs ``Saint Mary's CA'').
   \begin{itemize}
   \item Stage 1: exact match on normalized names against Kaggle lookup
   \item Stage 2: fuzzy match using Jaro-Winkler distance with threshold $0.3$
   \item All teams successfully matched in both divisions
   \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

# Past Strategies

## Academic Foundation
\begin{itemize}
\item Tournament seeding alone is a strong predictor via logistic regression with z-score transformation \cite{Schwertman}.
\vspace{0.15in}
\item Combined logistic regression and Markov chain models, benchmarked against nearly $100$ ranking systems, established logistic regression as the baseline standard \cite{Sokol2026}.
\vspace{0.15in}
\item No classifier (decision trees, random forests, naive Bayes, MLPs) exceeds $74$–$75\%$ accuracy on NCAAB data \cite{Zimmermann}.
\vspace{0.15in}
\item \textbf{Key takeaway:} feature construction matters more than model choice.
\end{itemize}

## Dominant Frameworks
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Fundamental Analysis:} construct a ``true" probability independent of public sentiment.
   \begin{itemize}
   \item Elo ratings \cite{chess}, KenPom, FiveThirtyEight, Massey
   \vspace{0.1in}
   \item Treats expert outputs as features, not final predictions
   \vspace{0.1in}
   \end{itemize}
\vspace{0.2in}
\item \textbf{Efficient Market Hypothesis} \cite{EMH}: betting markets aggregate information better than any single model.
   \begin{itemize}
   \item Uses closing lines from major bookmakers.
   \item \texttt{goto\_conversion} algorithm \cite{goto} corrects for favorite-long shot bias.
   \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

## NIL Era and Recent Baselines
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Boosting} \cite{raddar}: tiered features (seeding to efficiency to Elo to GLM team quality), implemented in XGBoost. Multiple top $10$ finishes in 2024 and 2025 cite his work as the baseline for their submission.
\vspace{0.15in}
\item \textbf{Simulation pipelines} among top 2024 finishers: predict point margins, then simulate brackets thousands of times via normal distribution over margins. 
\vspace{0.15in}
\item Inspired the three models in this paper: \textbf{Logistic Regression}, \textbf{XGBoost}, and \textbf{Linear Regression Monte Carlo}.
\end{itemize}

# Modeling Techniques

## Logistic Regression
\begin{itemize}
\item Binary classification model that applies the sigmoid function to a linear combination of features.
\end{itemize}
\vspace{0.1in}
\begin{equation}
P(Y=1 \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_k x_k)}}
\end{equation}
\vspace{0.05in}
\begin{itemize}
\item $\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \ldots, x_k)$: feature vector
\item $\boldsymbol{\beta} = (\beta_0, \ldots, \beta_k)$: coefficients estimated via maximum likelihood
\vspace{0.1in}
\item Output is bounded between $[0,1]$, making it interpretable as a probability.
\item Assumes linear relationship between features and log-odds; nonlinearity addressed via polynomial or interaction terms.
\end{itemize}
